topics.summary: Treat a whole tree and an individual item through the same operation. The attached EPUB motivates nested containers whose contents contribute to a combined result. blocks.text: Component declares the common query. Leaf answers directly. Composite stores Component connections, calls each child through that interface, and combines the answers. A child Composite repeats the same process. Recursion follows the tree; virtual dispatch chooses leaf work or another traversal. The caller does not need a separate query for every depth.

cards.question: What is Composite?
cards.answer: A design in which leaves and containers support the same useful operation over a tree.

cards.question: What is Leaf?
cards.answer: A tree node with no children.

cards.question: What is Recursion?
cards.answer: Solving a problem by calling the same operation on smaller parts until a stopping case is reached.

cards.question: What is Acyclic?
cards.answer: Having no path that leads back to an earlier node.

cards.question: Is Group still a Composite without Add, Remove, or IsComposite on Work?
cards.answer: Yes. Group implements Work and recursively queries Work children. Runtime editing and discovery are optional interface choices.

cards.question: Would copying the attached parent_ pointer into an owning smart pointer be safe?
cards.answer: No. The parent already owns downward in our tree. A strong owner back upward risks ownership cycles or double ownership; the parent link must be non-owning and kept consistent.

topics.title: A flat list works until a task contains tasks
topics.summary: A work plan contains steps measured in minutes. A step lasts from zero to ten thousand minutes. A group may contain steps and smaller groups. The tool must report the total for either a single step or an entire project. An empty group totals zero. A result above ten thousand minutes is rejected rather than silently accepted. This upper bound is a business rule and also makes integer arithmetic easy to reason about.

blocks.text: For a flat list, start with a vector of integers and a loop that adds them. Nothing about that problem requires a class family. The limitation arrives when groups can contain groups. Keeping one vector for steps and another for groups forces each caller to understand both types and every nesting level. A hard-coded loop for two levels fails as soon as a third group appears. We need one operation whose meaning stays valid at any depth.

topics.title: One operation for a part and a whole
topics.summary: Composite is a design for a tree whose individual items and containers support the same useful operation. A tree is a structure with one root and child branches, where following child links never leads back to an ancestor. A leaf has no children. In this example Step is a leaf, Group is a container, and Work is their shared contract. Work::minutes asks for total work time without asking which kind of object receives the request.

blocks.text: Step returns its stored duration. Group asks each child for its minutes and adds the answers. A child group repeats that process. This repeated call on a smaller part of the same problem is recursion. Recursion stops at a Step or an empty Group, so each valid finite tree eventually returns a result. A caller needs only one expression, work.minutes(), whether it measures one step or a project containing many groups.

The contract deliberately does not put add or remove on Work. Adding a child makes sense for a container but not for a leaf. Pretending every leaf can accept a child would create confusing no-op methods or runtime errors. Our groups receive their full child lists during construction and then expose only the query. That is enough for the current requirement and keeps the assembled topology stable.

topics.title: Build ownership from the leaves upward
topics.summary: Children is a type alias for a vector of unique_ptr<Work>. The vector owns its pointer objects, and each unique_ptr owns exactly one Work object. The virtual destructor in Work ensures that deleting through the base type destroys a complete Step or Group. When a group is destroyed, its vector destroys its children. Child groups then destroy their own children. The project owns the complete tree through a chain of clearly stated owners.

blocks.text: main first creates two Step objects for ten and twenty minutes. It moves their vector into a Group, then moves that child group into another vector alongside a five-minute Step. Finally it moves that vector into project. std::move permits ownership transfer; it does not copy the work objects. The source vector remains valid after its move, but the program does not depend on its size or contents. Its old children are now owned through the new container.

Group rejects a null child in its constructor. If validation throws, already-constructed member objects are destroyed automatically, including their owned children. No manual delete loop is needed. Since the public API only builds groups from completed children and does not later attach an existing group beneath a descendant, ordinary bottom-up construction yields an acyclic tree. This does not excuse creating a unique_ptr from an already-owned raw pointer; that would violate ownership rules before this API could protect the program.

topics.title: Follow the return values, not just the arrows
topics.summary: For the supplied project, the outer Group starts total at zero. Its first child is another Group. That inner group receives ten from its first leaf and twenty from its second, then returns thirty. The outer group adds thirty and next receives five. It returns thirty-five. Each group has its own local total. The locals exist in separate function calls, so the inner subtotal does not overwrite the outer subtotal.

blocks.text: In for (const auto& child : children_), the colon means take each element from children_ in sequence. child is a const reference to a unique_ptr already in the vector. It is not a copy; unique ownership must not be copied. The arrow in child->minutes() follows the pointer to the owned Work object and calls its virtual function. const on minutes says the operation does not change the tree through that interface. Every invocation computes fresh local state instead of storing a running total in a member.

Before adding n, Group checks whether n is greater than 10000 - total. If so, it throws overflow_error. Despite the exception name, the rejected condition here is the project's allowed budget, reached well before the built-in int limit. Testing before addition avoids doing an unsafe addition and only checking after damage. The nonnegative child contract makes the subtraction and comparison meaningful. A future Work implementation that returns negative minutes would break that contract even if its code compiled.

topics.title: Cost, depth, and the limits of uniform operations
topics.summary: The compiler checks that Step and Group provide minutes, and that an owning vector cannot be copied accidentally. At execution, virtual dispatch selects the correct child operation at each link. A complete query visits every node once, so its work grows in proportion to the number of nodes. Recursive calls use stack space proportional to tree depth. A million siblings and a million nested groups pose different risks: the latter may exhaust the call stack.

blocks.text: For an untrusted input format, enforce a depth limit while parsing or use an explicit stack for traversal. Our small, internally assembled tree has no parser and no arbitrary-depth guarantee. Caching a group total could make repeated reads cheaper, but would add invalidation concerns if editing later becomes possible. Since this tree is fixed after construction, storing a checked total at construction could also be reasonable when queries dominate. The example recomputes totals so the recursive mechanism stays visible.

Composite fits operations that make sense on both a part and a whole. A total duration qualifies. A command such as set_leaf_duration does not naturally apply to every container. Keep type-specific editing outside the uniform query contract. When maintaining the system, add a new leaf only after defining how it contributes to totals, ownership, and failure behavior. A new class name alone does not make a safe new component.

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Support nested groups and individual steps through Work::minutes.

blocks.text: A fixed tree with one shared query lets the same algorithm measure leaves and groups. Bottom-up construction and unique_ptr make lifetime clear.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: Every child is non-null and owned once.
Every successful child result is in the allowed nonnegative range.
A group visits each child once and does not retain a running total between calls.

blocks.text: Alternative: A flat vector is better when there is no nesting. A tagged value tree can avoid virtual functions for a closed set of node kinds, but every added kind then requires editing the variant-handling code.

Verification: The main program checks the 35-minute nested tree, an empty group, a 10000-minute leaf, a negative duration, a null child, and a 10001-minute group. It does not establish safe traversal of unbounded depth.
Maintenance: Project plans, scene trees, and nested UI elements benefit from uniform queries when their operations have meaningful leaf and group contracts.

topics.title: Chapter summary
topics.summary: Use these statements to explain the pattern from memory.

blocks.title: Main points
items: Composite gives parts and containers one meaningful contract.

workshop.title: A nested work plan
workshop.problem: A nested work plan. Support nested groups and individual steps through Work::minutes. Own every child exactly once; reject null children. Allow zero and totals through 10000; reject larger totals.

project=35 minutes
empty=0 minutes
invalid child, duration, and total rejected

steps.why: The first group adds its two leaf durations.
The outer group receives the inner result and adds five.
No children means the loop makes no additions.
One exceeds the remaining zero-minute budget.

workshop.pitfall: Store total as a member and add to it on every minutes call. For this nested tree, repeated queries return 35, then 100, instead of the same result. Both levels retain state: the inner group grows from 30 to 60, and the outer grows from 35 by adding 60 and 5.

discussion.question: The data is always a single flat list of durations. Should you use Composite? Give a concrete simpler representation.
discussion.answer: Use std::vector<int> with validated durations and a checked summing function. A tree and virtual query add little when no element contains other elements. Revisit Composite if nested groups become a real requirement.
discussion.hint: Remove abstractions when their motivating constraint disappears.

workshop.alternative: A flat vector is better when there is no nesting. A tagged value tree can avoid virtual functions for a closed set of node kinds, but every added kind then requires editing the variant-handling code.
workshop.design: A fixed tree with one shared query lets the same algorithm measure leaves and groups. Bottom-up construction and unique_ptr make lifetime clear.
invariants: Every child is non-null and owned once.
Every successful child result is in the allowed nonnegative range.
A group visits each child once and does not retain a running total between calls.
workshop.maintenance: Project plans, scene trees, and nested UI elements benefit from uniform queries when their operations have meaningful leaf and group contracts.

lab.task: Add a virtual steps() query returning the number of Step leaves beneath any Work object. A Step counts as one even when its duration is zero. An empty Group counts as zero. Preserve the duration query and every original test.
checks: The existing project has three steps and 35 minutes.
An empty Group has zero steps and zero minutes.
Step(0) has one step and zero minutes.
lab.answer: The solution gives Step a constant result and Group a recursive sum of child counts. The count is std::size_t, the container-size type. For the finite in-memory trees used here, the number of allocated nodes bounds the count. The duration and leaf-count operations stay separate because they answer different questions.

overview.title: The project owns a tree of work
overview.explanation: Ownership arrows point from owning Group to owned child. The Step block summarizes three distinct leaf objects, not one shared instance. The inheritance arrow describes the Group type, whereas the ownership links describe this example tree. Each child query returns a subtotal upward; ownership does not mean call direction.
